record.paper_title: Some Open Questions in Quiver Gauge Theory
record.original_question: What is a rigorous mathematical definition of Coulomb branches for 3d N = 4 gauge theories?

evidence.quote: Question 4. What is the mathematical definition of Coulomb branches (for 3d N = 4 theories)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. A three-dimensional N=4 supersymmetric gauge theory is specified, on the physical side, by a compact (or complex reductive) gauge group G together with a quaternionic (i.e. symplectic) representation M of G. To such a theory physicists associate a hyperkähler moduli space called the Coulomb branch, whose construction in physics involves a quantum-corrected metric and is not a priori algebro-geometric.

Problem. Give a rigorous mathematical definition of the Coulomb branch of a general 3-dimensional N=4 gauge theory as an algebro-geometric object. Concretely, for every pair (G, M) consisting of a complex reductive group G and a finite-dimensional symplectic representation M of G, construct in a functorial way:

(i) a complex affine Poisson variety M_C(G, M),
(ii) equipped with a ℂ^×-action of suitable weight on its coordinate ring,
(iii) whose generic symplectic leaf recovers the expected hyperkähler structure predicted by physics,
(iv) with a natural noncommutative deformation quantization (the quantized Coulomb branch),

such that the construction:
(a) reduces, in the case where M = N ⊕ N^* for some representation N of G, to the affine variety whose coordinate ring is the G((t))-equivariant Borel–Moore homology of the variety of triples (the BFN construction);
(b) is well-defined for arbitrary symplectic representations M (not necessarily of cotangent type);
(c) is compatible with known dualities and expected properties (e.g. symplectic singularities, the expected behaviour under Hamiltonian reduction, gauging, and 3d mirror symmetry).

State and prove a theorem providing such a definition, or determine whether such a uniform mathematical definition exists.
artifact.category_tag: Coulomb branches of 3d N=4 gauge theories
artifact.status_search_result: For gauge theories whose matter representation is of cotangent type N ⊕ N*, Braverman, Finkelberg and Nakajima gave a rigorous mathematical definition of the Coulomb branch as an affine Poisson variety, using equivariant Borel–Moore homology of a "variety of triples" (the BFN construction, 2015–2016). This has been widely developed since then (e.g. quiver cases related to slices in the affine Grassmannian). However, a fully general mathematical definition for arbitrary symplectic representations M (not of cotangent type), and one that uniformly captures all expected physical properties, is not yet available; the problem is therefore considered partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Towards a mathematical definition of Coulomb branches of 3-dimensional N=4 gauge theories, I
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes a mathematical definition of the coordinate ring of the Coulomb branch using vanishing cycle cohomology.
status_evidence.claim: Initial mathematical proposal for Coulomb branches.

status_evidence.title: Towards a mathematical definition of Coulomb branches of 3-dimensional N=4 gauge theories, II
status_evidence.snippet: Gives a mathematical definition of the Coulomb branch as an affine algebraic variety with C^×-action when the representation is of the form N ⊕ N*.
status_evidence.claim: BFN construction gives a definition in the cotangent (N ⊕ N*) case.

status_evidence.title: Coulomb branches of 3-dimensional gauge theories and related structures
status_evidence.snippet: Lecture notes surveying the BFN construction and remaining open problems for general symplectic representations.
status_evidence.claim: General case beyond cotangent type remains open.

status_evidence.title: Coulomb branches of 3d N=4 quiver gauge theories and slices in the affine Grassmannian
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies BFN Coulomb branches of quiver gauge theories with slices in the affine Grassmannian.
status_evidence.claim: Concrete identifications of BFN Coulomb branches in the quiver case.
